Apple is facing a civil lawsuit in Brazil, accused of allowing its App Store to let children download and access casino-style games without an effective age verification mechanism, with damages sought totalling 300 million reais (approximately US$59 million). Details of the incident are as follows.

Gambling Issues on Apple’s App Store in Brazil

Last month, Brazilian officials gave Apple five business days to provide further details explaining how it verifies gambling apps, how it monitors the App Store, and how it prevents minors from accessing age-restricted content.

The demand came three months after the National Secretariat for Digital Rights and the National Consumer Secretariat first made inquiries to Apple and Google regarding gambling apps allegedly accessible to children.

Days later, an investigation by 9to5Mac found around 100 apps disguising gambling platforms as innocuous games or tools to circumvent the App Store’s review process, many of which were available for children to download.

According to Tilt (via MacMagazine), Apple is now facing renewed scrutiny in Brazil over gambling apps on the App Store being accessible to minors.

The report states that Anced (the National Federation of Centers for the Defense of the Rights of Children and Adolescents), Educafro Brasil, and the Santo Dias Human Rights Center filed a civil lawsuit on 30 July, demanding that Apple set up an effective age verification system for all casino games distributed through the App Store.

According to Estadão, the plaintiffs are also seeking 300 million reais in moral damages.

The lawsuit mentions an app called "Casino Roulette: Roulettist," which claims to be for users aged 18 and over only, and points out that "during the process of accessing the content, no age verification, document checks, or facial recognition was ever required."

Tilt notes that the app offers a variety of casino games, including poker, baccarat, roulette, and slots, with in-app purchases of up to 599.90 reais, around US$118.

Although this is the only app directly named in the lawsuit, Anced’s representative lawyer claimed that "at least another six apps simulate casino operations, labelled as for users 18 and over, yet still available for minors to download."

In the lawsuit, the plaintiffs also demand that Apple prevent new casino games from being listed without age verification, continuously monitor existing games, and submit an enforcement report every six months.

If Apple fails to comply within 10 days, the groups are asking the court to impose a daily fine of 500,000 reais (approximately US$98,000).

When Tilt reached out to Apple for comment, Apple pointed to parental control options available through its Family Sharing feature and said it was testing an age verification system in Brazil, with plans to "roll it out to all users in the coming months via a software update."
